cards.statement: Mounting a filesystem over a populated directory hides that directory's existing entries.
cards.explanation: A mount covers the previous directory contents rather than erasing them. Unmounting reveals those contents again.

cards.statement: FHS forbids placing executable binaries under the `/etc` configuration hierarchy.
cards.explanation: FHS 3.0 limits /etc to static, local files that control how programs operate, and states that no binaries may be located under it.

cards.statement: On merged-usr systems, `/bin` holds separate copies of the executables in `/usr/bin`.
cards.explanation: On merged-usr systems, /bin is a compatibility symlink to /usr/bin, so both paths reach the same installed executables.
cards.misconception: The compatibility directory duplicates executable files.

source.title: UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy: version 0.1

cards.statement: FHS uses `/usr` as the standard parent directory for users' personal home directories.
cards.explanation: FHS assigns /usr to shareable installed resources, including commands, libraries and documentation, rather than personal home directories.
cards.misconception: The name /usr means that it contains user home directories.

cards.statement: FHS places changing system data, such as print spool contents, under `/var`.
cards.explanation: FHS uses /var for variable data, including spools, logs and administrative state that changes during operation.

cards.statement: FHS treats `/var/tmp` contents as temporary data to clear during system boot.
cards.explanation: FHS intends /var/tmp files to survive reboots. A site may still remove older files under its cleanup policy.
cards.misconception: Temporary files in /var/tmp are intended to be discarded at boot.

source.title: FHS 3.0: /var/tmp: Temporary files preserved between system reboots

cards.statement: Services use `/run` for current-boot runtime data, including local socket files.
cards.explanation: UAPI.9 describes /run as storage for runtime data and sockets that is cleared at boot, rather than retained service data.

source.title: UAPI.9 Linux File System Hierarchy: version 0.1

cards.statement: FHS assigns `/` as the recommended home directory for the root account.
cards.explanation: FHS recommends /root for the root account's home. It also permits the home location to be chosen by developers or local policy.
cards.misconception: The filesystem root is also the recommended home of the root account.

source.title: FHS 3.0: /root: Home directory for the root user

cards.statement: The kernel stores `/proc` process information as ordinary disk-backed files.
cards.explanation: Linux exposes process and system information through the virtual proc filesystem. Its entries are kernel interfaces rather than ordinary disk files.
cards.misconception: Process information under /proc is stored as conventional files on disk.

cards.statement: `df project/` totals the space consumed by files below the project directory.
cards.explanation: With a directory operand, df reports space usage for the filesystem containing that directory, rather than summing its subtree.
cards.misconception: A directory argument makes df calculate that directory tree's size.

cards.statement: Bash expands an unquoted `~/notes` using HOME when that variable is set.
cards.explanation: Bash substitutes HOME for a leading unquoted ~. If HOME is unset, it uses the executing user's home directory.

cards.statement: Writing to a file through one hard link changes the contents read through its other hard links.
cards.explanation: Hard links name the same inode and data. A write updates the shared file rather than an independent copy.

cards.statement: GNU ln can place a hard link on a different mounted filesystem from its target.
cards.explanation: Linux requires a hard link and its target to belong to the same mounted filesystem. A cross-filesystem link attempt fails.
cards.misconception: Hard links can connect files across mounted filesystems.

cards.statement: On Linux, the link() call returns an error when a root process asks it to hard-link a directory.
cards.explanation: Linux forbids directory hard links through link(). Administrative privilege does not provide an exception to that restriction.

cards.statement: GNU `ln -s` validates the target's existence before creating the new link.
cards.explanation: GNU ln -s accepts a target name that does not exist. The resulting symbolic link remains dangling until that name resolves.
cards.misconception: Creating a symbolic link requires an existing target.

cards.statement: Linux resolves a relative symlink target from the working directory where the link was created.
cards.explanation: A relative symbolic-link target starts from the directory containing the link. The link creation command's working directory is not recorded.
cards.misconception: Relative symlink targets retain the working directory used at creation.

cards.statement: `rm link` follows a symbolic link named link and removes the file it points to.
cards.explanation: For a symbolic-link operand such as link, rm removes the link itself. The referenced file remains in place.
cards.misconception: Removing a symbolic link with rm removes its referent.

cards.statement: A same-filesystem rename can leave an open file descriptor referring to the renamed file.
cards.explanation: Linux rename() changes a file's pathname while existing open file descriptors keep referring to that file.

cards.statement: With fs.protected_hardlinks=1, read access alone lets an unprivileged user hard-link another user's file.
cards.explanation: With protected_hardlinks enabled, ownership or read-and-write access is needed. Read access alone does not satisfy the nonowner access check.
cards.misconception: Read access alone satisfies protected_hardlinks for an unprivileged nonowner.

source.title: Linux kernel documentation: File system sysctls

cards.statement: Linux grants a file owner who is also in the file's group the union of the owner and group bits.
cards.explanation: Linux checks the owner class first: for the file's owner, only the owner permission bits decide access, even when the group bits would grant more.
cards.misconception: Owner and group permission bits combine when the owner belongs to the file's group.

cards.statement: A directory's read bit grants permission to traverse that directory during pathname lookup.
cards.explanation: For a directory, the execute bit grants access to the files inside it during lookup, while the read bit lets a user list the names it contains.
cards.misconception: Directory read permission also provides search permission.

source.title: GNU Coreutils manual: Structure of File Mode Bits

cards.statement: A file's write bit grants its owner permission to remove its name from the parent directory.
cards.explanation: Removing a file name needs write and search permission on the containing directory. The file's own write bit does not authorize that directory change.
cards.misconception: Write permission on a file authorizes deleting its directory entry.

cards.statement: `chmod 640 report` grants read permission to users who match the file's group class.
cards.explanation: The middle octal digit specifies the group permissions. A value of 4 supplies the group read bit.

cards.statement: GNU chmod's `a+X` grants execute permission on regular files that already have an execute bit.
cards.explanation: For a regular file, GNU chmod applies X when some execute bit is already set. This condition avoids making ordinary data files executable.

cards.statement: For a requested mode of 0666, `umask 000` can add execute permission to a new regular file.
cards.explanation: A umask removes requested permission bits; it does not introduce new ones. A requested mode of 0666 supplies no execute bits to preserve.
cards.misconception: A zero umask adds execute bits to the usual regular-file creation mode.

cards.statement: A file owner can give that file to another user with chown using ordinary owner permissions.
cards.explanation: Linux reserves ownership transfers for appropriately privileged processes. Mere file ownership does not grant that authority.
cards.misconception: File ownership includes the right to transfer ownership to another user.

cards.statement: `chmod 600 link` changes a Linux symbolic link's own mode bits.
cards.explanation: GNU chmod leaves symbolic-link permissions alone. For a symlink explicitly named on its command line, it changes the target's permissions.
cards.misconception: chmod changes the symbolic link's own permissions rather than the target's.

cards.statement: `bash script.sh` runs the commands in a readable script whose mode is 0644.
cards.explanation: Given as an argument, the file is opened and read by Bash, so read permission is enough. The execute bit matters when the script itself is run as a command, for example found through PATH.

cards.statement: For an unprivileged process, permission to chmod a file depends on owning it rather than on its write bit.
cards.explanation: chmod(2) requires the caller's effective UID to match the file's owner, unless the caller is privileged, so an owner can change the mode of a read-only file.

cards.statement: On Linux, the setuid bit gives a directly executed Bash script its owner's effective UID.
cards.explanation: Linux ignores the set-user-ID bit on interpreter scripts. Setting that bit on a Bash script does not provide its owner's effective UID.
cards.misconception: The setuid bit on a directly executed interpreter script changes its effective UID.

cards.statement: Linux can honor an ELF file's setuid bit when executing it from a nosuid mount.
cards.explanation: On a nosuid mount, set-user-ID bits confer no privilege. Linux may ignore the bits or refuse execution, depending on kernel behavior.
cards.misconception: A nosuid mount still permits setuid privilege changes for binary executables.

cards.statement: A new file automatically inherits the group of a setgid parent directory.
cards.explanation: Linux uses a setgid directory's group for files created inside it, rather than the creating process's effective group.

cards.statement: On Linux, changing an executable file's owner clears that file's set-user-ID bit.
cards.explanation: Linux clears set-user-ID when an executable changes ownership, including changes performed by root. The earlier permission setting does not persist.

cards.statement: Linux capabilities can give a process selected privileges while its effective UID stays greater than zero.
cards.explanation: Capabilities separate privileged operations into individual permissions. A process can hold particular capabilities rather than acquiring full root privilege.

cards.statement: With default sudoers policy, sudo asks for the target user's password when authentication is needed.
cards.explanation: By default, sudoers authenticates the invoking user rather than the target account. Policy options can change whose password is requested.
cards.misconception: sudo normally authenticates using the target account's password.

cards.statement: With util-linux su, `su - alice` starts the login shell in alice's home directory.
cards.explanation: The login option makes util-linux su change to the target user's home directory before starting the login shell.

cards.statement: `usermod -aG developers alice` retains alice's existing supplementary group memberships.
cards.explanation: The -a option appends the named groups to the current supplementary membership list. With -G alone, omitted memberships are removed.

cards.statement: Editing `/etc/group` automatically refreshes supplementary groups in existing login shells.
cards.explanation: Supplementary groups belong to process credentials. Editing the group database does not replace an existing shell's group list.
cards.misconception: A change in the group database immediately updates running processes' credentials.

cards.statement: A child created by Linux fork() initially uses the same working directory as its parent.
cards.explanation: fork() gives the child its parent's current working-directory setting, rather than resetting it to a home directory.

cards.statement: A process can get a fresh PID by replacing its program through Linux execve().
cards.explanation: Linux execve() replaces the program running inside an existing process. The process retains its PID across that replacement.
cards.misconception: Replacing a process's program also gives the process a new PID.

cards.statement: On a system booted with systemd, its system service manager runs as PID 1.
cards.explanation: systemd's system instance acts as the init process. Per-user systemd managers are separate instances rather than the system's PID 1.

source.title: systemd(1): Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: The procps-ng `ps` command can refresh its process listing periodically during a single run.
cards.explanation: procps-ng ps prints a snapshot of selected processes. Its manual directs users to top for a repeatedly updated display.
cards.misconception: ps itself provides a continuously refreshing process monitor.

cards.statement: Linux retains an exited zombie child's termination status for its parent to collect.
cards.explanation: A zombie has finished executing, but Linux keeps its termination information. A parent can collect that information and reap the child with wait().

cards.statement: Linux can reparent an orphaned process to a surviving ancestor configured as a child subreaper.
cards.explanation: When a parent exits, Linux selects the nearest living ancestor subreaper if one exists. The orphan then records that subreaper as its new parent.

cards.statement: Raising a Linux process's nice value gives it higher scheduling priority under normal scheduling.
cards.explanation: For normal Linux scheduling, a higher nice value means lower priority. The numeric nice value runs in the opposite direction from scheduling preference.
cards.misconception: A higher numeric nice value means higher scheduling priority.

cards.statement: An unprivileged Linux user can use renice to raise the nice value of a process they own.
cards.explanation: Linux permits an ordinary user to increase an owned process's nice value. This operation does not require administrative privilege.

cards.statement: Linux can send SIGTTIN when a background job tries to read from its controlling terminal.
cards.explanation: Terminal input normally belongs to the foreground process group. A background group's read attempt triggers SIGTTIN unless an exception applies.

cards.statement: Linux keeps a terminated process's PID reserved until the next system boot.
cards.explanation: Once a terminated process has been removed from the kernel process table, Linux can recycle its PID for another process, so a stored PID may later name an unrelated one.
cards.misconception: Process IDs remain reserved for the entire boot, even after the processes disappear.

cards.statement: `kill PID` sends SIGTERM by default when the caller supplies a positive process ID.
cards.explanation: kill selects SIGTERM as its default signal. Requesting a different signal requires an explicit signal argument.

cards.statement: A Linux process can catch SIGKILL to flush buffered output before it terminates.
cards.explanation: Linux does not allow a process to catch SIGKILL. That signal therefore offers the target no opportunity to run a cleanup handler.
cards.misconception: SIGKILL gives the target a chance to handle the signal and clean up.

cards.statement: With normal settings, the terminal driver sends SIGINT to the foreground process group on Ctrl-C.
cards.explanation: The terminal's interrupt character generates SIGINT for the foreground process group, so a foreground pipeline's processes receive the interrupt together.

cards.statement: With normal settings, the terminal driver uses SIGSTOP to suspend the foreground job on Ctrl-Z.
cards.explanation: The terminal's suspend character, usually Ctrl-Z, generates SIGTSTP. It is distinct from the SIGSTOP signal.
cards.misconception: Ctrl-Z generates SIGSTOP rather than SIGTSTP.

cards.statement: A successful `kill -0 PID` confirms that the target application is responding to requests.
cards.explanation: kill -0 checks that the target exists and that the caller has permission to signal it. It does not test the application's responsiveness.
cards.misconception: A successful zero-signal check is an application health check.

cards.statement: GNU `nohup command` automatically places command in the background of the invoking shell.
cards.explanation: GNU nohup changes hangup handling, not job placement. In a plain nohup command invocation, the shell still waits for the command to finish.
cards.misconception: nohup also launches the command as a background job.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command &` lets the shell continue while command runs as an asynchronous job.
cards.explanation: A trailing & makes Bash launch the command asynchronously. The shell proceeds to its next command rather than waiting for that job to complete.

cards.statement: In Bash, `bg %1` can resume a stopped job while the shell keeps control of the terminal.
cards.explanation: With job control enabled, Bash bg resumes the selected job in the background. The job remains outside the terminal's foreground process group.

cards.statement: An interactive Bash shell with its default signal handling exits when it receives SIGTERM.
cards.explanation: Interactive Bash ignores SIGTERM in the absence of traps. A script or a shell with customized signal handling is a different case.
cards.misconception: An interactive Bash shell follows the usual termination action for SIGTERM by default.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command >> log` appends standard output to an existing log file.
cards.explanation: Bash opens the target of >> for appending. Subsequent output goes at the end of the file, preserving the content already there.

cards.statement: With stdout on a terminal, Bash's `command 2>&1 > log` sends standard error into log.
cards.explanation: Bash applies redirections left to right. Here, 2>&1 first copies stdout's terminal destination; the later > log does not redirect that existing stderr destination.
cards.misconception: Duplicating stdout makes stderr track later changes to stdout's destination.

cards.statement: In Bash, `producer | consumer` passes producer's standard error through the pipe by default.
cards.explanation: A plain Bash pipe connects the producer's standard output to the consumer's standard input. Standard error keeps its separate destination.
cards.misconception: A plain pipe automatically combines standard output and standard error.

cards.statement: With pipefail set, Bash uses the rightmost failure's status for a failed `a | b | c` pipeline.
cards.explanation: Bash's pipefail option selects the rightmost nonzero command status. Rightmost refers to position in the pipeline, not which command finishes last.

cards.statement: With Bash noclobber off, `sort data > data` preserves data's original contents until sorting finishes.
cards.explanation: Bash opens and truncates data for output before starting sort. The input file is therefore already empty when sort begins reading it.
cards.misconception: The shell waits until sorting completes before overwriting the redirected input file.

cards.statement: In Bash, `<<'EOF'` lets a here-document contain literal `$HOME` text rather than the variable's value.
cards.explanation: Bash checks whether any part of a here-document's delimiter is quoted. A quoted delimiter suppresses expansions throughout the body.

cards.statement: Bash can pass an empty input stream to cat using the here-string `cat <<< ''`.
cards.explanation: Bash appends a newline to a here-string before supplying it as standard input. Even an empty supplied string therefore produces a newline byte.
cards.misconception: An empty here-string produces zero bytes of input.

cards.statement: In Bash, `value=$(producer)` removes trailing newlines from producer's captured standard output.
cards.explanation: Bash strips trailing newlines from output captured with $(). Newlines within the captured text remain.

cards.statement: In Bash, a builtin `cd` inside `$(...)` can change the outer shell's working directory.
cards.explanation: Bash runs $() commands in a subshell environment. A cd executed there leaves the surrounding shell's working directory unchanged.
cards.misconception: Commands inside $() share the surrounding shell's mutable working-directory state.

cards.statement: In Bash, `command >| log` overrides noclobber protection for an existing regular file.
cards.explanation: Bash's >| operator explicitly bypasses noclobber's protection against replacing an existing regular file. Other restrictions, such as filesystem permissions, still apply.

cards.statement: In Bash, `export REGION=west` puts REGION in the environment of later external commands.
cards.explanation: Bash marks an exported variable for inclusion in child-command environments. The command inherits its value at launch.

cards.statement: In Bash, `source ./settings.sh` can change variables in the current shell.
cards.explanation: Bash source executes a file's commands in the current shell context. Assignments there can therefore remain in that shell after the file finishes.

cards.statement: When Bash searches PATH for an executable, it chooses the last matching directory's executable.
cards.explanation: PATH is searched from beginning to end, and the first directory holding a matching file with execute permission wins, so earlier entries take precedence.
cards.misconception: Later PATH entries take precedence over earlier matching entries during a search.

cards.statement: In Bash, `tool "$@"` can preserve a separate argument for each positional parameter, including empty ones.
cards.explanation: Bash expands "$@" into separate arguments, retaining spaces and empty values within the original parameters. This preserves argument boundaries when forwarding them.

cards.statement: With default IFS in Bash, `items='red blue'; tool $items` passes red and blue as separate arguments.
cards.explanation: Bash applies word splitting to the unquoted expansion of items. The default IFS treats the space between red and blue as a separator.

cards.statement: For matching files, Bash's `ls *.log` lets ls turn the wildcard into filename arguments.
cards.explanation: When *.log matches files, Bash replaces the pattern with their names before invoking ls. ls receives the resulting filename arguments.
cards.misconception: The invoked command performs the shell's filename expansion.

cards.statement: Bash's default `*` expansion includes hidden names such as `.env` in the current directory.
cards.explanation: With Bash's default filename-expansion settings, * skips leading-dot names. Enabling dotglob includes those names in matching.
cards.misconception: The default star pattern includes hidden filenames.

cards.statement: With nullglob and failglob off, Bash passes an unmatched `*.log` pattern as a literal argument.
cards.explanation: Bash leaves a filename pattern unchanged when it has no matches and both nullglob and failglob are disabled. The command receives the pattern text itself.

cards.statement: Bash checks existing filenames to decide which words `{draft,final}.txt` expands into.
cards.explanation: Bash brace expansion generates draft.txt and final.txt textually. The existence of files with those names does not determine the generated words.
cards.misconception: Brace expansion selects names from the filesystem like filename matching does.

cards.statement: Bash returns status 126 when permission checks prevent execution of a command it has found.
cards.explanation: Bash reports a found-but-unexecutable command with status 126. A failed command search instead has status 127 under its normal command handling.

cards.statement: In Bash, `build && deploy` runs deploy when build exits with a failure status.
cards.explanation: Bash runs the command after && when the preceding command returns status zero. A failed build therefore prevents deploy in this list.
cards.misconception: The command after && runs in response to a failure of the preceding command.

cards.statement: GNU `grep -F 'a.b' file` treats the dot in the pattern as an ordinary character to match.
cards.explanation: With -F, GNU grep interprets the supplied pattern literally, including punctuation with special regex meanings.

cards.statement: GNU grep can use an unescaped `+` as a repetition operator in its default basic syntax.
cards.explanation: GNU grep's basic syntax uses \+ for repetition; grep -E uses an unescaped +.
cards.misconception: Basic and extended regex syntax use the same spelling for the repetition operator.

cards.statement: GNU `grep -c PATTERN file` can count repeated matches within one line as separate contributions.
cards.explanation: grep -c counts selected lines, so repeated matches within one line contribute a single count.
cards.misconception: grep -c totals matching occurrences rather than selected lines.

cards.statement: GNU `grep -r PATTERN link` can follow link when that symlink appears as a command-line operand.
cards.explanation: grep -r follows symlink operands but skips symlinks encountered during directory traversal.

cards.statement: After a successful scan with zero matching lines, GNU `grep PATTERN file` reports exit status 1.
cards.explanation: GNU grep uses status 1 for zero selected lines when the search completes without errors.

cards.statement: GNU `sed -n '3p' file` limits standard output to the third input line from file.
cards.explanation: GNU sed's -n suppresses automatic printing. The addressed p command explicitly prints the selected third line.

cards.statement: GNU sed creates a backup by default for `sed -i 's/old/new/' file`.
cards.explanation: GNU sed accepts -i with no suffix and makes no backup in that form. Appending a suffix, such as -i.bak, requests a backup.
cards.misconception: GNU sed's bare -i option creates a backup automatically.

cards.statement: With default input settings, gawk uses a newline to separate successive input records.
cards.explanation: gawk's default RS is a newline, so it normally reads and processes text one input line at a time.

cards.statement: In gawk, `$NF` evaluates to the number of fields in the current input record.
cards.explanation: For a record with fields, $NF gives the last field; NF holds how many fields the record contains.
cards.misconception: $NF gives the field count rather than the field at that index.

cards.statement: When gawk opens another input file, FNR continues counting from the preceding file's final record.
cards.explanation: FNR starts over for each input file, tracking the record position within that file.
cards.misconception: FNR is the cumulative record counter across the input files.

cards.statement: GNU find skips a following `-print` action when the adjacent preceding test evaluates to false.
cards.explanation: Adjacent find expressions imply conjunction. If the test fails, find short-circuits evaluation before the print action.

cards.statement: GNU `find . -type f -exec tool {} +` starts a separate tool process for each selected regular file.
cards.explanation: The + form batches multiple selected pathnames into a command invocation, subject to command-line size constraints.
cards.misconception: The + terminator gives the same per-file invocation behavior as the semicolon terminator.

cards.statement: GNU `find . -print0 | xargs -0 tool` can preserve filenames containing spaces or embedded newlines.
cards.explanation: find -print0 and xargs -0 agree on NUL-separated names. Spaces and newlines inside a name remain part of one argument.

cards.statement: GNU find visits a directory before its children when `-delete` is part of the expression.
cards.explanation: -delete enables -depth, which processes children before their directory. This order lets find remove a directory after its contents.
cards.misconception: Adding -delete leaves find's usual parent-before-children traversal order in place.

cards.statement: GNU xargs invokes echo by default when the caller supplies input but omits a command name.
cards.explanation: A bare GNU xargs passes its parsed input items to echo, which prints those items as arguments.

cards.statement: GNU `uniq file` can collapse identical lines even when a different input line separates their occurrences.
cards.explanation: GNU uniq collapses runs of adjacent identical lines. Identical lines in separate runs remain separate.
cards.misconception: uniq tracks previously seen lines throughout its input.

cards.statement: GNU `cut -d: -f2 records` extracts the second field from input lines that contain a colon.
cards.explanation: The -d option supplies the field separator and -f selects field positions. Here, cut chooses the second colon-delimited field.

cards.statement: GNU `tr 'ab' 'XY'` treats ab as one substring when choosing what input to translate.
cards.explanation: tr maps characters individually: a becomes X and b becomes Y, even when they appear apart in the input.
cards.misconception: tr matches whole strings rather than translating individual characters.

cards.statement: GNU `wc -l` counts a file's final unterminated text fragment as another input line.
cards.explanation: wc -l counts newline characters. A final text fragment that has no terminating newline adds nothing to that count.
cards.misconception: wc -l counts a final unterminated text fragment as a line.

cards.statement: GNU `tail -F app.log` can keep following app.log when log rotation replaces the file at that name.
cards.explanation: -F follows the file name and retries opening it, so tail can continue after a log file is removed and recreated.

cards.statement: GNU `tar -tf backup.tar` lists the member names stored in backup.tar.
cards.explanation: The -t operation inspects archive contents; -f identifies which archive GNU tar reads. Listing leaves the members archived.

cards.statement: GNU tar's `-J` option selects gzip compression for an archive operation.
cards.explanation: -J selects xz compression. GNU tar uses that compressor for archive creation or decompression.
cards.misconception: The uppercase -J compression option selects gzip.

cards.statement: By default, GNU tar removes a leading `/` from member names when creating an archive.
cards.explanation: GNU tar stores these names as relative paths by default; -P preserves their leading slash.

cards.statement: The `ssh-copy-id` command installs a user's private key on the remote account to enable key-based login.
cards.explanation: ssh-copy-id installs public keys in the remote account's authorized_keys file. The private key remains on the client.
cards.misconception: Key-based login needs the user's private key installed on the server.

cards.statement: OpenSSH can accept a changed key for a known host with `StrictHostKeyChecking=accept-new`.
cards.explanation: accept-new adds host keys for new hosts but rejects changed keys for known hosts.
cards.misconception: accept-new treats replacement keys for known hosts like keys from previously unknown hosts.

cards.statement: OpenSSH's `ssh -L 8080:db:5432 host` opens the forwarding listener on the remote host.
cards.explanation: The -L listener runs on the client machine. The remote SSH side connects to db:5432 for connections accepted by that listener.
cards.misconception: -L puts the listening port on the remote SSH host.

cards.statement: Since OpenSSH 9.0, the scp client uses the SFTP protocol by default for remote file transfers.
cards.explanation: OpenSSH 9.0 changed scp's transfer default to SFTP. The -O option explicitly requests the legacy SCP protocol.
cards.volatilityNote: A future OpenSSH release could change scp's default transfer protocol.

cards.statement: APT can fetch a requested package's missing dependencies from configured repositories during installation.
cards.explanation: APT's installation commands resolve package dependencies and retrieve required packages from the configured sources.

cards.statement: On Debian, `apt update` upgrades installed packages to versions listed in the repositories.
cards.explanation: apt update refreshes package information from configured sources. Upgrading installed packages is a separate operation.
cards.misconception: apt update installs the newer package versions it discovers.

cards.statement: Debian's apt(8) recommends the `apt` command as the stable interface for package-management scripts.
cards.explanation: Debian's apt(8) recommends apt-get or apt-cache for scripts. apt targets interactive use and can change behavior between versions.
cards.misconception: apt is the recommended stable interface for scripts.

source.title: apt(8): Script usage and differences from other APT tools

cards.statement: On Fedora 41 and later, the `dnf` command runs DNF5 by default for package-management operations.
cards.explanation: Fedora's switch makes /usr/bin/dnf point to /usr/bin/dnf5, so the familiar command invokes DNF5.
cards.volatilityNote: A future Fedora release could choose a different provider for the dnf command.

cards.statement: A systemd timer can run a shell command from its own `ExecStart=` setting when the schedule elapses.
cards.explanation: A timer schedules activation of another unit, normally the service with the same base name. The timer does not execute a shell command itself.
cards.misconception: A timer stores its scheduled command in its own ExecStart= setting.

source.title: systemd.timer: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: For matching system unit filenames, systemd prefers `/etc/systemd/system` over `/usr/lib/systemd/system`.
cards.explanation: systemd loads administrator unit files before vendor files of the same name, letting local configuration override the packaged definition.

source.title: systemd.unit: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: By default, `systemctl edit api.service` opens the vendor unit file for direct modification.
cards.explanation: By default, systemctl edit creates or edits a drop-in override, such as api.service.d/override.conf, leaving the vendor unit file intact.
cards.misconception: systemctl edit changes the packaged unit file directly by default.

source.title: systemctl: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: Running `systemctl enable api.service` brings an inactive api.service into the running state.
cards.explanation: enable prepares activation through the unit's installation links. Starting an inactive service also needs start, or enable --now.
cards.misconception: Enabling a service also starts its current instance.

source.title: systemctl: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: systemd refuses to start a masked service when another unit pulls it in as a dependency.
cards.explanation: Masking points the unit file to /dev/null, blocking activation. Disabling removes installation links but leaves other activation routes available.

source.title: systemctl: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: With default kill settings, systemd sends SIGTERM before using SIGKILL on a service that fails to stop.
cards.explanation: systemd initially sends KillSignal=, whose default is SIGTERM. If processes remain after the stop timeout, its default final signal is SIGKILL.

source.title: systemd.kill: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: With `Restart=on-failure`, systemd restarts a `Type=simple` service by default after SIGTERM kills its main process.
cards.explanation: For Type=simple services, systemd counts SIGTERM termination as clean by default. Restart=on-failure therefore does not restart the service for that signal.
cards.misconception: Restart=on-failure treats SIGTERM termination as a service failure.

source.title: systemd.service: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: The `journalctl -u api.service` command selects journal entries associated with api.service.
cards.explanation: journalctl -u filters for the named unit, including its messages and related messages emitted by the system manager.

source.title: journalctl: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: Running a bare `journalctl -b` shows the log messages recorded during the previous boot.
cards.explanation: With an empty argument, journalctl -b shows the current boot. An offset such as journalctl -b -1 selects the boot before it.
cards.misconception: Omitting journalctl's boot argument selects the previous boot.

source.title: journalctl: Official manual source, systemd v262

cards.statement: With `Storage=volatile`, systemd-journald keeps its journal files under `/var/log/journal`.
cards.explanation: Storage=volatile directs new journal data to /run/log/journal, using runtime storage rather than the persistent journal path.
cards.misconception: The volatile storage setting writes new journals to the persistent directory.
